name: Tessera Corponation Ossified Dead Drop Node
product_name: Tessera Corponation Ossified Dead Drop Node
description:
The Ossified Dead Drop Node is a passive communication device encased in a ceramic-composite shell engineered to be structurally and thermally indistinguishable from common urban debris — broken concrete, poured aggregate, architectural rubble. The Node contains a compressed data storage core, a short-range inductive reader interface, and a tamper-dissolution charge that renders the storage medium unreadable upon unauthorized physical breach. It holds no active transmitter. It broadcasts nothing. It simply waits.

Tessera's engineering philosophy here is radically conservative: the Node operates on the assumption that any active transmission, no matter how encrypted, is a liability. Instead, the Node accepts data uploads and downloads exclusively through direct inductive contact �� a paired reader passed within three centimeters of the Node's surface. The exchange takes between 0.4 and 2.1 seconds depending on payload size. The Node logs contact timestamps and can be configured to self-dissolve after a set number of accesses, a fixed time window, or upon detection of unauthorized spectral scanning above a defined threshold.

Nodes are typically placed by one party and retrieved or read by another — the classic dead drop model, hardened against the digital surveillance architecture of GLMZ. Tessera manufactures them ostensibly for 'secure physical data archival in high-risk construction environments,' a designation that satisfies municipal licensing requirements while doing nothing to obscure the product's actual market. They are found embedded in walls, tucked into drainage infrastructure, mortared into the gaps of older precinct buildings, and buried in parks. The city is full of them.

cultural_context: The Reliquary has a particular romance in GLMZ's underground — the idea of the city itself as a message system, its walls and gutters threaded with silent information. There are hobbyist communities that hunt for Nodes, mapping their locations and attempting to read them — a pastime that sits in legal grey territory and occasionally turns dangerous when a Node proves to belong to someone territorial. Among professional operatives, placing a well-concealed Node in a location that survives for months is a point of quiet pride. There are stories — probably apocryphal — of Nodes placed during the city's last major restructuring period that are still active, still holding data that no one alive knows how to retrieve.
known_users: Political dissidents organizing across precinct lines
story_hooks: A player inadvertently leans against a wall and their inductive reader — active for an unrelated purpose — downloads 4GB of encrypted data from a Node that had been waiting there for eleven months.
A Node the players planted has been accessed twice by an unknown party before its intended recipient arrived — someone knew it was there.

A dying contact presses a reader into a player's hand and gives only a street intersection before losing consciousness. The Node at that location contains something that multiple parties are already moving to retrieve.
A node-hunter collective approaches the players for protection — they found a Node that dissolved before they could read it, and now someone is following them, apparently convinced they already did.

A Tessera Corponation internal audit reveals that a production run of Nodes was shipped with a hidden secondary inductive interface — a backdoor that allows Tessera to read any Node in that batch remotely, at range, without triggering the tamper charge.
